blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Tokenizers are usually treated as fixed preprocessing tools, but they are trained on text and can retain traces of that text in their vocabularies. We ask whether a BPE tokenizer can reveal if a candidate dataset was part of its training corpus. The key observation is simple. Rare strings become tokens only when enough corpus frequency pushes them over the merge threshold. This suggests that membership signal should appear in rare tokens used by the candidate dataset, rather than in the order in which merges were made. We formalize this under a threshold model of BPE inclusion, showing that the likelihood-ratio test assigns its largest weights to tokens that are rare in the background but frequent in the candidate dataset. The same model suggests that merge rank and merge-graph position should not add a first-order membership signal once token existence and dataset frequency are known. We instantiate this view as RTAM-Fusion, which calibrates rare-token mass with shadow tokenizers and combines signals across rarity levels. On the tokenizer membership benchmark, RTAM-Fusion improves AUC and balanced accuracy over Vocabulary Overlap while using fewer shadow tokenizers. Existing defenses also continue to leak membership signal against adaptive attackers at production vocabulary sizes. Code: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/RTAM-Fusion-F7EE/

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Tokenizers are usually treated as a fixed first step before modelling begins.
Text is split into token IDs, and the language model is then trained on those IDs.
This view misses an important point. Subword tokenizers are themselves learned
from text. A BPE tokenizer builds its vocabulary by deciding which strings occur
often enough in the training corpus to become tokens. The tokenizer is therefore
not only a preprocessing tool, but also a data-dependent artifact that may retain
traces of the corpus used to train it. More broadly, securing generative AI systems requires examining vulnerabilities beyond conventional model performance. Mustafa et al. (2025) ; Shen et al. (2024) ; Yazmyradov (2024) ; Mustafa et al. (2026) demonstrate that even relatively simple prompt-based jailbreaks can circumvent safety mechanisms in language and text-to-image models, highlighting the importance of evaluating security under adversarial conditions. While these attacks concern generation-time safeguards rather than training-data privacy, they illustrate the broader need to investigate overlooked attack surfaces. In this work, we focus on one such surface: the information retained by a tokenizer during training.

We ask what part of the tokenizer actually carries this signal. Several answers
seem plausible. A member dataset may share unusual vocabulary items with the
target tokenizer. Its tokens may appear at distinctive merge ranks. Its merge
graph may have a recognizable structure. Or it may simply be compressed in a
different way. Our results point to a simpler explanation. For dataset-level
membership, the signal is mainly in rare tokens that the candidate dataset
activates.

blocks.en:
The intuition is direct. Common strings become tokens regardless of whether one
particular dataset was present, so their existence says little about membership.
Rare strings are different. If a candidate dataset repeatedly uses a rare string,
and that string appears in the learned vocabulary, then the dataset may have
helped push it over the frequency threshold needed for inclusion. The useful
quantity is therefore not just whether the vocabulary overlaps with the dataset,
but how much of the dataset’s own token stream falls on rare learned tokens.

We formalize this intuition under a threshold model of BPE inclusion. Under this
model, the likelihood-ratio test for tokenizer membership assigns its largest
weights to tokens that are rare in the background corpus but frequent in the
candidate dataset. This motivates a rarity-weighted statistic over the dataset’s
activated-token mass. The same model also suggests that merge rank and merge-graph
position should not provide an independent membership channel once token existence
and the dataset’s own token frequencies are known. In short, rarity matters more
than order.

principle Carlini et al. (2022) , and combine them into one membership
score. The threat model is the same as in Tong et al. Tong et al. (2026) .
The change is the statistic used to read the tokenizer.

TPR@1%FPR comparisons. We keep this distinction explicit because low false
positive rates are important in membership inference.

The same view also clarifies why some defenses are brittle. If merge order is not
where the signal lives, then randomizing merge order should not remove the signal.
We test this by evaluating defenses against attackers that know the defense was
applied and adapt their features. Across targeted removal of member-distinctive
tokens, min-count filtering, merge-order randomization, and a bounded per-site
contribution mechanism, the tested defenses do not drive membership inference to
chance at production vocabulary size. Removing rare tokens weakens the original
signal, but can leave a fragmentation footprint that an attacker can
read.

blocks.en:
Overall, our results show that tokenizer tokens tell training tales through rare
vocabulary entries. We make three contributions. First, we characterize the
membership signal in BPE tokenizers with a threshold inclusion model, which
predicts that rare tokens activated by the candidate dataset carry the main
signal, while merge order and merge-graph position should not add a first-order
channel. Second, we introduce RTAM-Fusion , a calibrated rare-token
activation mass attack that improves AUC and balanced accuracy over the strongest
published tokenizer membership baseline while using fewer shadow tokenizers.
Third, we evaluate tokenizer defenses against adaptive attackers and show that
the tested defenses still leak membership signal at production vocabulary size.

blocks.en: 2 Related Work
blocks.zh: 2 相关工作

blocks.en:
Membership inference asks whether a candidate example, document, or dataset was
part of training. Most work studies this through a trained model. We study a
different released artifact, the tokenizer. This changes the signal: a language
model exposes losses, probabilities, or generations, while a tokenizer exposes a
learned vocabulary.

Membership inference and calibration. Shokri et al. Shokri et al. (2017) introduced the shadow-model paradigm,
where an attacker trains models on known member and non-member splits and learns
to classify the target’s outputs. Later work showed that raw membership scores
are often confounded by example difficulty. Yeom et al. Yeom et al. (2018) connected membership advantage to the generalization gap, Salem
et al. Salem et al. (2019) reduced the assumptions needed for attacks, and
Sablayrolles et al. Sablayrolles et al. (2019) derived an optimal membership
rule using per-example thresholds. Watson et al. Watson et al. (2022) and Ye et al. Ye et al. (2022) further developed calibrated
hypothesis-testing views. Carlini et al. Carlini et al. (2022) introduced LiRA, which calibrates a target example against reference models, and
Zarifzadeh et al. Zarifzadeh et al. (2024) reduced the number of reference
models needed. We inherit this calibration principle, but not the object being
calibrated. A tokenizer has no loss or confidence score, so we calibrate
rare-token activation mass against an out-shadow tokenizer null.

membership is carried by token existence and rarity.

blocks.en:
Tokenizer membership inference. Tong et al. Tong et al. (2026) introduce membership inference against
tokenizers and define the shadow-tokenizer threat model we adopt. They propose
Compression Rate, Naive Bayes, Merge Similarity, Vocabulary Overlap, and
Frequency Estimation. Vocabulary Overlap is their strongest attack and counts
distinctive candidate tokens present in the target vocabulary. Frequency
Estimation is also related, since it scores rank-frequency deviations. In our
terms, both are existence-family methods. Merge Similarity and Compression Rate use order or compression signals and are
weaker in their experiments. Our analysis gives one explanation for this pattern.
Under a threshold model of BPE inclusion, the likelihood-ratio form emphasizes
tokens that are rare in the background but frequent in the candidate dataset.
The same model predicts that merge order and merge-graph position should not add
a first-order membership signal once token existence and candidate-token
frequency are known. RTAM-Fusion is therefore a calibrated,
rarity-weighted version of the signal used implicitly by the strongest prior
tokenizer attacks.

Defenses and adaptive evaluation. The same distinction matters for defenses. Minimum-count filtering limits the
influence of rare events, echoing sensitivity control in differential
privacy Dwork et al. (2006) . Randomized merge selection is related to
the exponential mechanism McSherry and Talwar (2007) and to private learning
methods such as DP-SGD Abadi et al. (2016) . Targeted token removal resembles
machine unlearning Cao and Yang (2015) ; Bourtoule et al. (2021) . Tong
et al. Tong et al. (2026) evaluate min-count filtering and merge-order
randomization against static attacks. We evaluate these and related mechanisms
against adaptive attackers. This matters because a defense may remove one
statistic without removing the underlying signal. In our experiments, order
randomization does not help because order is not the membership channel, and
content removal leaves a fragmentation footprint that an adaptive attacker can
read.

blocks.en: 4.3 Why merge order is not used

blocks.en:
The target tokenizer also exposes merge ranks, and one might expect these ranks
to contain membership information. Our analysis suggests that, for dataset-level
membership, this is not the main channel. Merge order is mostly governed by the
global frequency ordering of the corpus. A single candidate dataset can affect
membership evidence when it pushes a rare token over the inclusion threshold, but
that effect is already captured by token existence and the candidate dataset’s
own token frequencies.

blocks.en:
This proposition is a model implication rather than a finite-sample theorem about
all BPE runs. It says that once we know which candidate tokens exist and how much
the dataset uses them, merge order should not provide an independent membership
channel. This is why RTAM-Fusion deliberately uses existence and
frequency-derived features, even though merge indices are available in the threat
model.

频道. 这就是为什么RTAM-Fusion 故意使用存在和

blocks.en:
The proposition also gives a testable prediction. Order-based and merge-graph
attacks should not outperform rare-token existence statistics unless they capture
some additional signal outside this model. In Section 5 , we
find that such attacks remain close to chance, while rare-token activation
features carry the membership signal.

blocks.en: 4.4 Implications for defenses
blocks.zh: 4.4 对辩护的影响

blocks.en:
The same distinction matters for defenses. If merge order is not the membership
channel, then randomizing merge order should not remove the signal used by an
adaptive attacker. Defenses that remove rare vocabulary entries are more direct:
they can weaken the original rare-token signal. But removal can also change how
member datasets are re-tokenized after pruning, leaving a fragmentation footprint
that a different adaptive statistic can exploit.
We therefore do not claim an impossibility theorem for tokenizer defenses. The
theory supports a narrower claim. Rare token existence is the first-order
membership signal under the threshold model, and defenses should be evaluated
against attackers that can adapt to whatever signal remains. The experiments in
Section 5 test this prediction directly.

同样的区别对辩护来说也是重要的。 如果合并顺序不是会员
通道,然后随机排列合并顺序,不应删除一个

blocks.en: 6 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 6 结论

blocks.en:
Tokenizers are not neutral preprocessing tools. They are learned from text, and
their vocabularies can retain traces of the corpora that trained them. This paper
showed that, for BPE tokenizer membership inference, the strongest signal comes
from rare tokens activated by a candidate dataset. Merge order and merge-graph
structure are not where the main membership evidence lives. This observation led
to RTAM-Fusion , a calibrated rare-token activation mass attack that
improves AUC and balanced accuracy over the strongest published baseline while
using fewer shadow tokenizers. The low false-positive regime is more mixed, with
the clearest gains at production vocabulary sizes. The defense results tell the
same story from the other side. Randomizing merge order does little because order
is not the channel. Removing rare tokens can weaken the original signal, but it
can also leave a fragmentation footprint that an adaptive attacker can read. Our
study is limited to BPE tokenizers and the site-level C4 benchmark, so
cross-tokenizer, out-of-distribution, and canary-style evaluations remain
important next steps. Tokenizer tokens tell
training tales, even when weights are never queried.

blocks.en: Limitations
blocks.zh: 限制

blocks.en: This study focuses on BPE tokenizers and on the site-level C4 benchmark used in prior tokenizer membership work. The threshold model in Section 4 is an explanatory model for this setting, not a complete account of tokenizer training. Real BPE changes the alphabet as merges are learned, and token inclusion events are dependent because tokens compete for a fixed vocabulary budget. Our results should therefore be read as evidence that rare-token existence is the main membership channel in this benchmark, not as a finite-sample optimality claim for every tokenizer. Several evaluations remain open, including other tokenizer families such as WordPiece, unigram tokenizers, and SentencePiece variants, along with out-of-distribution, cross-corpus, and canary-style tests. Our defense results are limited to min-count pruning, merge-order randomization, targeted token removal, and bounded per-site contribution. None drives adaptive membership inference to chance at production vocabulary size, but this does not show that tokenizer defenses are impossible. We also do not evaluate content-level differentially private tokenizer training, where noise is applied to token counts during learning rather than after the vocabulary has already been built. Finally, our attack assumes that the adversary can train shadow tokenizers from a similar broad distribution and knows the tokenizer training procedure, matching the prior benchmark but not every deployment setting.

blocks.en: C.4 Implications for defenses
blocks.zh: C.4 对辩护的影响

blocks.en:
The theory suggests two expectations for defenses. First, a defense that changes
only merge order should not remove the main membership channel. The likelihood
ratio in Theorem 1 depends on token existence and rarity, not
on the order in which surviving tokens were created.
blocks.zh:
该理论对防御提出了两个期望. 首先,一个改变的辩护
仅合并顺序不应去除主会员频道. 可能性
定理1中的比例取决于象征的存在和稀有性,而不是
以创造活物的顺序排列。

blocks.en:
Second, defenses that remove vocabulary content can reduce the original
rare-token signal, but they may create a different signal. If a member dataset
previously used a distinctive token and that token is removed, the dataset must be
re-tokenized into smaller pieces. This can change its tokenization pattern more
than it changes the pattern of a non-member dataset that did not rely on the
removed token. We call this a fragmentation footprint.

We do not formalize this footprint as a theorem. Doing so would require a model
of how BPE re-tokenizes strings after token removal, together with a separate
detection-theoretic analysis for the footprint statistic. Instead, we treat it as
a mechanism suggested by the theory and tested empirically in the adaptive-defense
experiments.

blocks.en: C.5 Scope
blocks.zh: C.5 范围

blocks.en:
The theory supports three claims. First, under the threshold model, the optimal
existence-based membership test gives the largest weight to tokens that are rare
in the background and frequent in the candidate dataset. Second, RTAM-style
features are calibrated, finite-sample approximations to this likelihood-ratio
structure. Third, merge order and merge-graph features are not expected to add
membership signal once token existence and candidate-token frequency are known.

The theory does not claim that RTAM-Fusion is exactly optimal for finite
BPE training. It also does not claim that no tokenizer defense can work. Real BPE
uses an evolving vocabulary, token-existence events are dependent, and
content-removal defenses require a separate model of re-tokenization after
pruning. We use the theory as a characterization of the main membership channel
and as a guide for the adaptive evaluations, not as a complete impossibility
result.
